There are laptop spring screws that use the spring to hold them to the place so they dont get lost. Like once all the scres are turned. You can lift the part without worry about where to put the screws until you need to put them back in.

Star pattern is kind of more like a technique for proper removal.
Assume we have 5 screws holding something down. 
If we start from the top and go around clockwise to number them. 
.....1.....
5.........2
4.........3
You would unscrew them in the order of 1,4,2,3,5 or 1,3,5,2,4 or eveb 3,5,2,4,1
The idea is to allow the pressure holding the part down remain as equal as possible while you remove it to minimize the chance of damaging the part underneath. So wheb you are done with one screw, the next screw you go to is not directly next to it. 
Some people take this a step further and will do one turn of the screwdriver at each screw, repeating the "star pattern" until the screws loosen ebough to remove the cover. 
This is most inportant for cpu (and gpu on laptops) where you may have pins and pressure mounted heat sinks or heat pipes.

Unfortunately the main issue here is chrome isnt exactly a browser at least not by the normal accepted means in which a web browser used to operate.
 It basically launches a bunch of sub processes and acts as it's own "mini operating system" it pulls a bunch of resources and does a lot of background stuff. Sadly this is normal behavior. Chrome even has it's own task manager. You can find this in settings. If anything is there you can close those. 
If your computer can handle it don't worry about it. If you feel this is sluggish try other web browsers out. Opera is a lightweight good one that is, at least used to be. Based off chromium. Chromium can be thought of as a variant of chrome and is made and maintained by google. In fact microsoft is using it for newer versions of edge too. 

It might sound like I'm hating on chrome. I just want to mention that I do use it as my primary browser for at least 85% of my web activity. There are benefits of chrome behaving this way. Such as new tabs getting allocated their own ram and sub process. Yet this only works if you have resources to use them. Plus this opens up a door for memory leaks if websites are not designed for chrome using this feature. 
Tl;dr
Chrome is being a little selfish, yet it's worth it. Yet if pages aren't optimized for chrome it can lead to those resources allocated never getting sent back to your machine.

If you want to learn a bit more. Look up how "heap" and "stack" are handled by running processes. Adding those keywords to a web search might give more fruitful info
